title: Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods
claim: Pulling the surrogate posterior back into a statistical manifold yields a gradient bound that explains where acquisition gradients vanish.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, curved arrows linking boxed regions across panels, shared bottom legend
description: Three side-by-side line and scatter plots share a legend strip along the bottom. Left, "Surrogate and AF": a GP mean with a blue confidence band over a brown true function. A yellow-to-purple LogEI strip runs along the bottom. Markers show the observed data point, the best point (red diamond), the next point (yellow star), and a green cross. Middle, "AF gradient bound": log-scale curves for the AF gradient (magenta), the upper bound (dashed blue), and tr(FIM) (red), plus a cyan baseline. Dashed gray boxes in the left and middle panels are linked by curved gray arrows. Right, "Posterior map": points plotted by mean against log standard deviation, forming two arches colored by LogEI. The same markers appear on the arches. The eye goes first to the colorful arches on the right.
caption: Left: GP surrogate (SE kernel) and LogEI [ref] acquisition function. Middle: visualization of the upper bound for the acquisition function gradient from Proposition [ref]. Right: induced geometry on the input space by the posterior map in the statistical manifold defined by predictive mean and standard deviation. The color bar represents the same LogEI as in the left panel. Distant inputs can have similar predictions. Gray regions contain no observations and have a small pullback trace.
abstract: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) through the lens of information geometry. Pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map yields a local sensitivity tensor on the input space, which leads to an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions (AFs). This view explains vanishing-gradient behavior in high-dimensional BO and provides a common interpretation of heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales. The upper bound can also serve as a generic recipe to understand the behavior of new acquisition functions or surrogates in high input dimensions as well. Using the bounds, we also identify necessary conditions for an input location to be an optimizer of the AF for a univariate Gaussian predictive posterior. Building on this analysis, we propose FITR, a trust-region-based BO method that replaces lengthscale-based scaling with local pullback-Fisher weights. FITR is not restricted to GP kernels with explicit lengthscales and easily generalizes to non-isotropic surrogates. FITR shows competitive performance on several benchmarks.
